title: Putin’s chief negotiator vows to seize ‘every inch of Russian land’ in Ukraine
gist: US-brokered Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi (first direct talks in nearly a year) produced only a tentative prisoner swap; Russia still demands Ukraine leave the remaining 10% of Donbas, and negotiator Medinsky vowed 'every inch of Russian land' will be returned. Dickinson argues Putin's 'historically Russian lands' ideology makes a Donbas-only deal illusory and peace possible only through strength.

themes.theme: Abu Dhabi talks: optimism vs substance

insights.claim: The first direct Russia–Ukraine negotiations in nearly a year, US-brokered in Abu Dhabi over two days, ended without breakthroughs beyond tentative agreement on a major prisoner exchange.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Peace-deal headlines are not backed by substance; fade ceasefire-driven rallies in Ukraine-linked assets.
insights.locator: The first direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine

insights.claim: Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said the talks provided 'good momentum' and suggested a solution might be reached by year-end, but the author sees little evidence for such optimism.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Author's view: year-end peace timelines are unrealistic.
insights.quote: there is little evidence to support such optimistic assessments
insights.locator: At this stage, there is little evidence

insights.claim: Ukraine proposes the current front lines as the basis for a territorial settlement, while Russia demands Ukraine also withdraw from the remaining 10 percent of the Donbas still under Kyiv's control.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: The Donbas withdrawal demand is the core sticking point; any shift on it is the signal to watch.
insights.quote: withdraw from the remaining 10 percent of the Donbas region
insights.locator: At this stage, there is little evidence

insights.claim: Ukraine resists ceding the rest of the Donbas because it contains a fortress belt of cities critical for national defense, whose surrender would leave the rest of the country exposed to further Russian advances.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Explains why a land-for-peace deal on Donbas is militarily near-unacceptable for Kyiv.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s reluctance to retreat from the Donbas

themes.theme: Medinsky's maximalism and Russia's constitutional claims

insights.claim: Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky said 'Every inch of Russian land will be returned to Russia, one way or another' on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi talks.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Signals Moscow's maximalist negotiating posture remains intact.
insights.quote: “Every inch of Russian land will be returned to Russia, one way or another,”

insights.claim: Russia amended its constitution in 2022 to include all of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces, none of which it fully occupies, so 'Russian land' could mean far more than the remaining Donbas.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Constitutional claims cap Kremlin flexibility; a Donbas-only settlement would not satisfy formal Russian claims.

insights.claim: Putin said in October 2026 of Ukraine's occupied regions: 'I think it is not their territory, but the historical territory of Russia.'
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Reinforces that Kremlin goals are ideological, limiting compromise space.
insights.quote: “I think it is not their territory, but the historical territory of Russia,”
insights.locator: In all likelihood, Russia’s chief negotiator

themes.theme: Why a Donbas-focused peace deal is likely illusory

insights.claim: The author argues that while US officials focus talks on the Donbas, Putin has much bigger goals, and Donbas is a stepping stone toward controlling all of Ukraine including Kyiv.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: A land-for-peace deal would likely be temporary; war risk persists beyond any Donbas settlement.
insights.quote: it seems self-evident that Putin has much bigger goals in mind

insights.claim: Putin's objections to European troops in postwar Ukraine and efforts to cap Ukraine's military size indicate he is setting conditions for the next stage of invasion rather than seeking peace.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Watch security-guarantee terms (European troops, army caps) as the real test of a durable deal.
insights.quote: everything seems designed to create favorable conditions for the next stage of Russia’s invasion
insights.locator: There are many red flags signaling

insights.claim: Russian demands to address the war's 'root causes' read like a playbook to undermine Ukrainian sovereignty, leading many to conclude Putin sees Ukraine's existence as the root cause.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: 'Root causes' language in talks should be read as a non-starter signal.

insights.claim: Putin's 'historically Russian lands' rhetoric sounds unhinged internationally but is routine for the Russian public, having been made a central pillar of national discourse.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Domestic legitimacy of imperial aims reduces the chance of Kremlin moderation even under economic pressure.
insights.locator: This belief is not Putin’s alone.

insights.claim: The author concludes Putin will not be swayed by limited territorial gains or short-term economic incentives, so peace is only possible through strength.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Implies continued Western military support and defense spending rather than an incentive-based settlement.
insights.quote: Peace is still possible in such circumstances, but it must be peace through strength.
insights.locator: Anyone who wants to broker a peace deal
